question.prompt:
If \(a_2\ne0\) and \(r,\) \(s\) are the roots of \(a_0+a_1x+a_2x^2=0,\) then the equality

\[ \begin{aligned} a_0+a_1x+a_2x^2 &=a_0\left(1-\frac xr\right)\\ &\quad\cdot\left(1-\frac xs\right) \end{aligned} \]

holds:

solutions.explanation:
The roots appear in denominators, so we must first determine when neither root is zero. Since \(r\) and \(s\) are the two roots of a quadratic with leading coefficient \(a_2\ne0\), its root factorization is
\[
a_0+a_1x+a_2x^2=a_2(x-r)(x-s).
\]
This includes the case of a repeated root. Substituting \(x=0\) gives
\[
a_0=a_2rs.
\]
Consequently, if \(a_0\ne0\), both \(r\) and \(s\) are nonzero. We can then rewrite the proposed right side as
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_0\left(1-\frac xr\right)\left(1-\frac xs\right)
&=\frac{a_0}{rs}(x-r)(x-s)\\
&=a_2(x-r)(x-s).
\end{aligned}
\]
This equals the original quadratic for every \(x\), including \(x=r\) and \(x=s\).

If \(a_0=0\), then \(rs=0\), so at least one denominator in the proposed expression is zero. Multiplication by \(a_0=0\) does not make that undefined expression meaningful. Therefore the identity holds for all \(x\) provided \(a_0\ne0\), choice A.
solutions.title: Factor the quadratic and check the denominators
